short: Rome's northernmost frontier in Britain was abandoned within two decades of completion.
full:
Antoninus Pius ordered a new turf wall built from 142 CE across the narrow waist of Scotland between the Firth of Clyde and the Firth of Forth, roughly 100 miles north of Hadrian's Wall, seeking a military success to bolster his legitimacy early in his reign. Governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus oversaw construction of a turf rampart on a stone base, fronted by a ditch and studded with forts roughly every two miles.

The wall never matched Hadrian's in scale or garrison density, and sustained pressure from northern tribes made it costly to hold. Rome abandoned it around 162, shortly after Antoninus Pius's death, withdrawing the garrison back to Hadrian's Wall, which resumed its role as the permanent frontier. A brief reoccupation under Septimius Severus around 208 proved equally temporary, and the Antonine Wall never again functioned as an active Roman boundary.
